---
title: "Open-Set Recognition"
description: "A recognition setting in which a model must classify known classes while detecting inputs from classes it did not learn."
term: "Open-Set Recognition"
letter: "O"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Advanced"
---

## Simple explanation

In ordinary classification, a model is generally expected to choose among
the classes it knows. Open-set recognition also asks the model to recognize
when an input may belong to none of those known classes.

## Technical explanation

Open-set recognition separates a set of known classes from unknown or
unseen classes. A system may assign known labels to familiar inputs and
reject or flag examples that do not sufficiently match known classes.
This differs from closed-set classification, where every test example is
assumed to belong to one of the trained classes.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Real deployments encounter inputs beyond the training taxonomy. Rejecting
uncertain or unfamiliar cases can reduce confident misclassification and
route examples for human review, but threshold choices determine the trade
off between rejecting known examples and accepting unknown ones.

## How it works

Methods may use distance in a learned representation, calibrated
confidence, explicit unknown-class training data, or specialized scoring
rules. The system compares a score to a decision threshold and can abstain
when evidence for known classes is insufficient. Evaluation should include
unknown classes not seen during training.

## Practical example

A wildlife classifier trained on five bird species could flag a deer image
as unknown rather than incorrectly forcing it into one of the five bird
labels. It should also be tested on new bird species and challenging
images of known species.

## Common misconceptions

- Open-set recognition is not solved simply by adding an "unknown" label if representative unknown examples are unavailable.
- Low confidence is a useful signal but does not guarantee that an input is unfamiliar.
- Open-set recognition and out-of-distribution detection are related but describe different problem formulations.
